clue.text: Recover ground engineers surrender

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
to capitulate is to give in to an enemy

explanation.surface: Army engineers give up the ground they had just won back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recover ground' looks military, but it means go over the same points again, as in a summary.
explanation.definitionFit: To sum up is to go back over territory already covered, which is what recovering ground means figuratively.

clue.text: Tackle fraudulent manipulation

explanation.surface: Equipment is used for cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's ropes and gear are its tackle; fixing an election or result dishonestly is also called this.

clue.text: Artist in fashion, or manager 'of gallery

indicators.note: the artist's letters are placed inside the word for fashion

parts.note: to fashion or shape is to cut
RA, Royal Academician, is the standard abbreviation for an artist

explanation.surface: A trendy painter, or else the person running the gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: The keeper responsible for a museum's collection is its custodian, the person in charge of what is shown.

clue.text: Even great actor leaves producer

parts.note: even, as in level, means plane
Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a celebrated Victorian actor-manager

explanation.surface: Even a famous actor walks out on the theatre producer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' reads as a verb in the surface; it is the noun, foliage, so the definition is something that produces leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A deciduous shade species common in London streets bears foliage, so it is a producer of leaves.

clue.text: Derelict ship

explanation.surface: An abandoned vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagrant or down-and-out is a derelict; a cargo vessel with no fixed route is a tramp steamer.

clue.text: Be careful, watching Jack

explanation.surface: Watch your step: someone named Jack is observing.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack is a sailor (Jack Tar); a sailor posted to keep watch is the lookout.
explanation.definitionFit: The warning 'watch it!' means take care; the sailor on watch from the crow's nest is also so called.

clue.text: Platform for plebeian representative

explanation.surface: A political platform for a man of the people.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised dais for speakers is a tribune; in ancient Rome an official elected to protect the commons was also one.

clue.text: Paraphrased in order, to make short? I wonder

indicators.note: putting letters in order rearranges them, so these words are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Someone muses on whether a paraphrase is meant to shorten a text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in order' shuffles the letters of SHORT and I WONDER together.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something in a different way is restating it, which is what a paraphrase does.

clue.text: Return appearance, for example, in African part

indicators.note: the whole string built from the pieces is read from end to start

parts.note: an air is a look or appearance
EG, exempli gratia, means for example
taken as written

explanation.surface: A return visit, for instance, to part of Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' turns the whole run AIR + EG + IN backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A West African country is part of that continent.

clue.text: Unfriendly spies also ordered outside

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the spies
the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: Hostile spies are also given their orders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spies' reads as the subject of the surface sentence, but it only supplies the American agency's initials, and 'outside' wraps the reshuffled letters round them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who avoids company and is not sociable is unfriendly.

clue.text: How things are developing for rural invention?

explanation.surface: A question about how farming innovations are progressing.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means the current state of affairs; read literally, a falsehood (invention) about the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the prevailing situation; cryptically, an untruth told about farmland.

clue.text: Alter list in the plant

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are placed within the word the

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to alter is to change, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Change the list of what is in the plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alter' makes ISTL from LIST, which goes 'in' THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A prickly weed, Scotland's emblem, is a kind of plant.

clue.text: Extravagant academic exploit

parts.note: a professor is an academic, PROF for short
to exploit something is to use it

explanation.surface: A lavish professor takes advantage.
explanation.definitionFit: Lavish or abundant, given in great quantities, is extravagant.

clue.text: Mountain where counter-productive German loses head

indicators.note: the first letter of the German's name is dropped

parts.note: Hans Geiger, German physicist, produced the Geiger counter

explanation.surface: A German who undermines his own efforts loses his head on a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'counter-productive' seems to mean self-defeating; it means one who produced a counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous Swiss Alpine peak with a notorious north face is a mountain.

clue.text: Best fare — nothing minced — for dinner

indicators.note: mincing chops something up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: The best food, with nothing chopped up, for the evening meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional British Sunday joint is a dinner.

clue.text: A cross on top of church in Devon

indicators.note: in a down answer the cross sits above the church

parts.note: a cross is the letter X
a minster is a large church

explanation.surface: A cross mounted on top of a church in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the bare 'in Devon': a town there, Devon being a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in the south-west English county, famous for its carpets, lies in Devon.

clue.text: Tree makes naturalist smile

parts.note: Gilbert White was an English naturalist of Selborne
to beam is to smile broadly

explanation.surface: A tree brings a smile to a nature lover.
explanation.definitionFit: A European tree of the rose family with pale-backed leaves is a tree.

clue.text: Bad mark repeated in one exam

indicators.note: the doubled letters are placed within the word built from one and exam

parts.note: one is I in Roman numerals
an oral is a spoken exam

indicators.note: the letter for mark appears twice

parts.note: M is short for mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A poor mark is given twice in a single exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked, lacking morals, is a sense of bad.

clue.text: No use going mad about half-a dozen committing deadly sin

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go around the number
going mad suggests disorder, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: six is VI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: No use losing your temper over six people committing a mortal sin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going mad' makes ENOUS from NO USE, and 'about' puts it round VI.
explanation.definitionFit: Envy is one of the seven deadly sins, so someone feeling it is committing one.

clue.text: Detect snag in contract

explanation.surface: Spot a problem in an agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot someone in the act is to detect them; a hidden drawback in a deal is also so called.

clue.text: Warn an amusing sort

explanation.surface: Warn a funny person.
explanation.definitionFit: To admonish is to warn; an entertaining, mischievous person is called 'a real' one.

clue.text: Dreads troublesome children.

explanation.surface: Fears unruly kids.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrors are dreads or fears; unruly youngsters are called little terrors.

clue.text: Dismissal in cricket ground seen by about 1000

indicators.note: the ground comes beside, just after, the other pieces

parts.note: re means about or concerning
M is 1000 in Roman numerals
the Oval is a London cricket ground

explanation.surface: A batsman's dismissal at a cricket ground watched by some thousand spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a wicket falling; the definition is dismissal from a post.
explanation.definitionFit: Being taken away from a job or post is being dismissed.

clue.text: Contemplating part Shakespeare knew little of

indicators.note: only a portion of the word contemplating is used

explanation.surface: Thinking about a role Shakespeare knew little about.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson said Shakespeare had 'small Latin and less Greek'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonson's tribute mocks the playwright's scant classical language learning.

clue.text: Not involved in fight, so not charged

explanation.surface: Someone stays out of a fight and so avoids prosecution.
explanation.definitionFit: A country taking no side in a war is non-aligned; a particle with no electric charge is also so called.

clue.text: Fashioned as court garment for knight

indicators.note: fashioned means shaped anew, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Made as a court robe for a knight.
explanation.definitionFit: A tunic worn over armour by a medieval knight is his garment.

clue.text: Attempt, say, to preserve what's old hat

indicators.note: say signals that the word for attempt is spoken

parts.note: an attempt is a try
to corn meat is to preserve it in salt

explanation.surface: A try, as it were, to keep something that is out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old hat' means outdated, but here it is literal: a hat of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-cornered cocked hat of the eighteenth century is an old style of hat.

clue.text: Maintaining solidarity in concluding lincs

parts.note: concluding means ending or closing
ranks are lines of soldiers

explanation.surface: Staying united at the end of a set of lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers tightening up their formation is the image behind a group standing together.
